newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada auto union talks stuck over outsourcing.
newsitem.headline: Canada auto union talks stuck over outsourcing.

text.p: Canadian Auto Workers (CAW) union president Buzz Hargrove said on Monday that talks to settle a new collective agreement at Chrysler Corp 's Canadian unit were grinding slowly over outsourcing.

"My major concern today is that there is really no indication that Chrysler's prepared to reduce to writing anything that restricts their ability to make decisions on outsourcing," Hargrove said in a telephone interview. He said the talks, which began last week, were also bogged down by a surprise proposal from the automaker on profit-sharing.
"Chrysler threw a curve at us," he said. "It certainly stirred a hornet's nest up with our chairman on our Chrysler committee."
Hargrove said Chrysler committee chairman Ken Lewenza was angry with the profit-sharing proposal. But Hargrove added that he did not believe Chrysler was serious unless it wanted a strike.

"If it's a serious demand on their part then it becomes a show-stopper," he said. In 1984 the CAW split from the United Auto Workers and held a two-week strike over a similar demand on profit-sharing from General Motors Corp.
Chrysler said its proposal on gain-sharing was not up for discussion in the press.

"We don't do our negotiating through the media," said Othmar Stein, vice president of public affairs for Chrysler Canada. But he suggested that Chrysler's proposal could tie wage rises to quality and production targets.
"I'm not saying that's our position. But that's how it works at other companies," Stein said.
The union said Chrysler's proposal came in response to the CAW's proposal over the weekend for a three percent wage increase in each year of a three-year deal.
Meanwhile, the UAW in the United States began talks over the weekend with its negotiating target, Ford Motor Co.
Labor contracts in Canada and the United States expire on September 14, but UAW president Stephen Yokich has not chosen a strike deadline and continues low-level talks with Chrysler and GM.
The CAW is the largest private sector union in Canada, with 52,800 of its 210,000 members in the auto industry.

Negotiators are trying to craft a proposal that could form the basis of an agreement between the union and Chrysler and set the pattern for collective agreements at the other two North American carmaking operations in Canada.
The CAW has said it was prepared to strike for its demands if a deal was not reached by the September 17 deadline.
This round of bargaining may be different because General Motors Canada Ltd has threatened to resist a pattern agreement that does not meet its needs in the area of outsourcing work.
Outsourcing is the sale of plants or the transfer of work to outside contractors, whose employees are not generally members of the auto unions.

The union said GM had made outsourcing decisions in the past year in which it would sell two of its plants in Canada and eliminate more than 5,000 CAW jobs. The union has said it was determined to try and reverse the decisions.
